digests.narrative:
This is the theme he is most invested in personally and the one where his crowd-sourced channel work did the most this week. Community checks from CIOE Shenzhen confirmed Sivers has raised laser prices and that the 70mW grade tied to 800G pluggables is the tightest, with Innolight checks showing ASPs rising across the entire 70mW to 200mW range. He reads rising prices flowing through to gross margin in coming quarters as the mechanism.

The framing he has adopted, borrowed from a Citi TMT note, is that lasers and optical fibre are being positioned as the next HBM and will carry a scarcity premium. He expects the 2027-2028 photonics cycle to look like memory's 2025-2026. Sivers gave that argument its hardest number by committing USD 30m to Glasgow for capacity above 100 million CW DFB lasers annually, operational in Q4 2027, which he modelled against historical pricing as a $625m-$1.25bn revenue ceiling.

He also surfaced the structural point that matters most and read it only one way: Coherent has withdrawn from merchant indium phosphide laser supply and expects to buy in some datacom over time. He treats that as bullish for the remaining merchant suppliers, which it is.
keyPoints: CIOE Shenzhen channel checks: Sivers confirmed raising laser prices; 70mW is the tightest grade
Innolight checks put ASPs rising across the whole 70mW-200mW range, not one part
Citi TMT frames lasers and optical fibre as the next HBM, with a scarcity premium
Sivers committed USD 30m to Glasgow for over 100 million CW DFB lasers, operational Q4 2027
Coherent has withdrawn from merchant laser supply — tighter for everyone else still selling
He expects the 2027-2028 photonics cycle to rhyme with memory's 2025-2026

digests.narrative:
His memory conviction hardened rather than moderated, and the week gave him the cleanest confirmation yet that the shortage has pricing power beyond the memory makers themselves. HBM scarcity is reported to have driven AI accelerator prices in China up 20-50%, with Huawei's Ascend 950DT repriced above quotes from two months earlier and Cambricon's 690 up 20-30%. His response — that as someone long memory he is happy about causing this much inflation — is the honest version of the trade: the memory makers are taxing everyone downstream.

He sizes it with TrendForce placing DRAM and NAND at 68% of hyperscaler capex in 2027, and argues that when procurement at that scale lands on balance sheets carrying 70-80% margins, short-term macro scares do not matter. The legacy tier remains his favourite second-order expression, where he owns ESMT and Etron outright and compares ESMT's trajectory to Sandisk's.

This was also the only theme the market agreed with. Memory names rose sharply over the month while photonics and materials fell hard, which is the first time this year his highest-conviction theme and the tape have pointed the same way at the same time.
keyPoints: HBM scarcity pushed Chinese accelerator prices up 20-50%: Huawei's Ascend 950DT and Cambricon's 690
TrendForce puts DRAM and NAND at 68% of hyperscaler capex in 2027
He reads memory-driven inflation in end-product pricing as confirmation, not as a warning
Legacy tier is the second-order trade: he owns ESMT and Etron and compares ESMT to Sandisk
Situational Awareness bought options across SK hynix and Sandisk into high implied volatility
Memory names rallied hard while the rest of the chain fell — the only theme the market paid for

digests.narrative:
His framing this week was geopolitical rather than operational, and it favours the incumbents. He laid out where the genuine chokepoints sit and the striking thing is how few are American: ASML in EUV with Zeiss and Trumpf beneath it, Soitec in photonics-SOI, and a Japanese cluster holding 90-100% share across EUV photoresist, coat and develop, actinic mask inspection, mask blanks and specialty glass. The United States holds EDA, some equipment and the downstream giants; Taiwan and Korea hold the manufacturing; China's leverage is upstream in gallium, graphite and refined lithium rather than in fabrication.

Within that he names TSMC among his five favourite megacaps and says he has maintained the bullish stance for over a year despite Intel and Samsung competition, on the grounds that it is the centre of the AI buildout and has demonstrated it can raise prices straight into margin. He also flagged Intel reportedly lifting PC CPU prices 10% in October as something markets should welcome.

One tape observation he keeps returning to: Taiwanese names recovered far faster than US or European ones through the September drawdown, which he reads as local investors caring less about macro than about order books.
keyPoints: He maps the real monopolies and finds almost none are American: ASML in EUV, Soitec in photonics-SOI
A Japanese cluster holds 90-100% share in EUV photoresist, coat/develop, mask inspection and blanks
China's leverage is upstream inputs — gallium, graphite, refined lithium — not manufacturing
TSMC is his pick of the megacaps: the centre of the buildout, with demonstrated pricing power
Intel reportedly raising PC CPU prices 10% in October, which he thinks the market will like
Taiwan equities recovered far faster than US or EU names through the September drawdown

digests.narrative:
The category's central bear case has always been residual value: rented GPUs depreciating faster than the contracts can pay for them. Oracle's disclosure that renewing GPU capacity resold at a 20% premium, on equipment mostly four years and older, is the first realised-price evidence against it, and he read it across to Nebius and IREN immediately.

Nebius also retains the company-specific catalyst from the week before, with Palantir naming it a preferred sovereign AI infrastructure partner and routing existing government and enterprise relationships toward its capacity. That remains a designation rather than a disclosed contract value, so there is still no revenue number attached.

His broader point is that frontier demand keeps outrunning the ecosystem's ability to build, with Anthropic's $35bn compute deal with NVIDIA-backed Lambda as the template, and he expects more such deals to land on neocloud and colocation operators.
keyPoints: Oracle resold renewing GPU capacity at a 20% premium on four-year-old-plus equipment
He reads this across to Nebius and IREN as residual-value support for the whole category
Palantir named Nebius its preferred sovereign AI infrastructure partner
Still a designation rather than a disclosed contract value
Frontier demand keeps outrunning capacity — Anthropic's $35bn Lambda deal is the template

digests.narrative:
The substrate layer got third-party validation of the thesis he has argued longest. Bloomberg reported that indium phosphide substrates are emerging as a key risk for the semiconductor industry, and his response was simply to point out he had said so a year earlier through AXT. Indium phosphide is the base material under the lasers the whole photonics theme depends on, and it is now being described as an industry-level risk rather than a niche supply problem.

The same week supplied the other half of that story. China reportedly halted some rare earth shipments to the United States, with no blanket ban announced and no named materials, so he used Japan as the indicator: gallium, dysprosium, terbium and yttrium imports from China stood at zero in June, Shin-Etsu suspended new orders for dysprosium-bearing magnets, and Proterial had received no Chinese export licences. Reuters' account named indium phosphide among historical targets.

He does not treat these as opposing facts. Scarcity and jurisdiction risk are the same story to him — the material gets dearer and harder to move at the same time, and the owner of the capacity captures the price.
keyPoints: Bloomberg reported indium phosphide substrates emerging as a key risk for the industry
He notes he identified that chokepoint through AXT roughly a year earlier
China reportedly halted some rare earth shipments to the US; Reuters named InP among past targets
Japan's gallium, dysprosium, terbium and yttrium imports from China stood at zero in June
Shin-Etsu suspended new orders for dysprosium-bearing magnets; Proterial had no export licences
AXT remains his best-performing idea, up roughly 3000% over a year

digests.narrative:
Broadcom's quarter was the centre of his week and he read the selloff as an overreaction. Guidance of roughly $115bn of AI revenue in FY27 and $230bn in FY28 is near 100% growth in both years against a street modelling about $180bn, management said demand actually exceeds that outlook, and the company put itself on target to exceed $30 of earnings per share in fiscal 2028 — which he points out is under twelve times forward at the price. The line he singled out for this theme specifically is that AI networking revenue should grow just as fast as XPUs.

Broadcom then supplied the most useful evidence of the week about somebody else's business. Its chief executive said demand for lasers, whether EML or CW, is far surpassing supply across the industry — and said it while tripling Broadcom's own laser capacity.

From Marvell he took two things at Semicon Taiwan: its optical engineering lead naming Europe and Japan as laser sourcing geographies rather than the US, which he reads as pointing at the one listed European merchant supplier of scale; and a transition timeline putting near-packaged optics at late 2027 to 2028 with full co-packaged optics after that.
keyPoints: Broadcom guides AI revenue to about $115bn in FY27 and $230bn in FY28, against a street near $180bn
Management said it is on target to exceed $30 EPS in fiscal 2028 — under twelve times forward
AI networking revenue is expected to grow just as fast as XPUs over the next few years
Broadcom's CEO said laser demand far surpasses supply, while tripling its own laser capacity
Marvell's optical CTO named Europe and Japan for laser sourcing at Semicon Taiwan, not the US
Marvell puts near-packaged optics at late 2027-2028, with full co-packaged optics after

digests.narrative:
This card changes shape this week: LPKF moves into the glass layer from materials, so the theme finally contains the name through which glass-substrate progress actually reaches the book. It is still only two tickers.

The news is a delay, and it is the analyst reporting a setback in his own theme, which is the kind of disclosure worth weighting heavily. Samsung Electro-Mechanics has delayed its semiconductor glass substrate investment on a bottleneck in customer reliability evaluations of prototypes, revising the start of operations to 2028, with SKC also pushing back. For an equipment supplier this is worse than it is for a substrate maker: the tool order lands before the line runs, so a customer moving its start date right moves LPKF's revenue with it, and there is no partial credit. The share price is down about 12% on the month, which is the market reading the same thing.

Corning remains the other half of the card and has not moved: its glass-bridge case rests on 2028 fibre array unit TAM rather than anything shipping, and co-packaged optics delay reports weigh on that and the FAU case together. Conviction stays low. Glass is a 2028-2029 layer on current evidence, and the datapoint that would change this card is a disclosed tool order from a named substrate customer with a delivery year attached — not another timeline article.
keyPoints: LPK.DE re-categorised into glass from materials — the layer now holds the equipment exposure directly
Samsung Electro-Mechanics delays glass substrate start of operations to 2028; SKC also pushes back
Equipment leads the line, so a customer's slip moves LPKF's revenue event with it
LPK.DE is down about 12% on the month against a flat tape
GLW's glass-bridge case still rests on 2028 FAU TAM rather than current shipments
What would change the card: a disclosed LIDE order from a named customer with a delivery year

digests.narrative:
He treats humanoids as the next major theme after space and AI, and is explicit that he wants downstream leaders rather than component suppliers until volumes scale. Agility is the position he is trying to build, on the argument that an application-specific approach already deployed in Amazon and Mercado Libre warehouses is further along commercially than the general-purpose programmes — his line being that a robot does not need to do backflips to do packaging and delivery work.

The new material this period came from Chinese channel checks on which components resist domestic substitution: planetary roller screws top the list with the lowest substitution rate, followed by 6D force sensors and dexterous hands. He presents these as moats worth knowing rather than as positions, consistent with his preference for staying downstream.

He remains explicitly sceptical on Tesla as robotics exposure: Optimus is not pure-play, and the general-purpose approach is unproven. Its appearances in his feed are mostly as a holding he mentions in passing rather than as a thesis.
keyPoints: He wants downstream humanoid leaders, not upstream component suppliers, until volumes scale
Agility is framed as ahead on commercialisation via Amazon and Mercado Libre warehouse deployments
China channel checks: planetary roller screws show the lowest domestic substitution rate
6D force sensors and dexterous hands also resist domestic substitution — he reads these as moats
Explicitly sceptical on Tesla: Optimus is not pure-play exposure and general purpose is unproven

digests.narrative:
The week's most decision-relevant item for him was second-hand: Oracle disclosed that all GPU capacity coming up for renewal was resold at a 20% premium to previous contracts, on equipment mostly four years and older. He reads that as a direct falsification of the rapid-depreciation bear case, and it is the strongest evidence yet on that specific question because it is realised pricing on used capacity rather than a forecast.

His structural case is unchanged: NVIDIA's 70% growth figure is what it believes it can supply rather than what is demanded, roughly $1.3T of hyperscaler capex is projected for 2027, and inference has overtaken training after being roughly even eighteen months ago. He also argues there will be no regulatory slowdown, assigning essentially zero probability to Anthropic or OpenAI easing frontier development and reading most proposed rules as regulatory capture.

Worth noting because it is rare: he added a hedge, saying he would be more cautious on 2027. That is the first time this desk has recorded him qualifying the accelerator position at all.
keyPoints: Oracle resold renewing GPU capacity at a 20% premium on equipment four years and older
He reads that as directly falsifying the rapid GPU depreciation thesis
NVIDIA's 70% growth is a supply statement; unconstrained growth would exceed 100%
Roughly $1.3T of hyperscaler capex projected for 2027, excluding SpaceX
He assigns essentially zero probability to any frontier lab slowing development
He is more cautious on 2027 than on 2026 — the first hedge he has put on this name

digests.narrative:
He treats this group as the demand floor rather than as investments, and his argument this week was about the durability of the spending rather than its size. He points to $127bn of 2027 Anthropic and OpenAI training and inference spend drawn from internal investor documents, notes that SpaceX is excluded from the $1.3T hyperscaler capex figure so the real total may surprise, and adds that the Pentagon is reportedly looking at $5bn into Fluidstack — state money entering a build that had been entirely corporate.

His timing framework comes from Anthropic's published economic scenarios, which show little separation between outcomes through 2027 and sharp divergence into 2028-2030. He maps that onto capex directly: 2026-2027 are buildout years, so free-cash-flow headwinds now are the price of profitability later, and he says so explicitly for Amazon, Meta and Alphabet.

Amazon remains his most-cited name here, continuing to accumulate silicon exposure through Qualcomm warrants tied to as much as $60bn of milestone revenue. What he does not discuss anywhere is how the capex is being financed.
keyPoints: He cites $127bn of 2027 Anthropic and OpenAI training and inference spend from internal documents
SpaceX capex is excluded from the $1.3T figure, so the true total may be higher than quoted
The Pentagon is reported looking at $5bn into Fluidstack — state money entering the buildout
Anthropic's scenarios put little separation through 2027, then sharp divergence into 2028-2030
He accepts near-term free-cash-flow damage as the price of post-2028 profitability
Amazon keeps buying silicon exposure: Qualcomm warrants tied to up to $60bn of milestone revenue

digests.narrative:
This layer exists because the desk built it, not because the feed produced it. Every thesis that touches power reaches it through a list rather than an argument. Bloom Energy is the only sustained name: it appears in a late-July recap for 166% year-on-year revenue growth with expanding margins and raised 2026 guidance, and again in the note that grid power bottlenecks triggered a five-fold increase, to $25B, in Brookfield's financing for its fuel cells. That financing line is the clearest power-constraint datapoint anywhere in the feed.

The second thread is a components one and sits mostly outside the US listed set: a shortage of high-power cylindrical cells for battery backup units, with Samsung SDI supplying Simplo, which assembles for Meta and Amazon, and both Panasonic and Samsung reported short. Vertiv, Eaton, EnerSys and BorgWarner are named only as adjacent read-throughs, and the analyst says plainly it is outside his domain.

GE Vernova and Constellation carry no analyst mentions at all, which is exactly the tiering caveat this layer was built to expose: grid interconnection, transformers and on-site generation are load-bearing for every gigawatt in the neocloud and hyperscaler digests, and the feed prices none of it. Conviction is low because the evidence is thin, not because the constraint is.
keyPoints: Desk-built layer: no thesis in the feed argues power directly, only in passing
BE is the only sustained name — 166% YoY revenue growth, raised 2026 guidance
Grid power bottlenecks drove a 5x increase, to $25B, in Brookfield's financing for BE fuel cells
A BBU cylindrical-cell shortage runs through Samsung SDI, Panasonic and Murata, with no direct US listing
VRT, ETN and ENS appear only as adjacent read-throughs, explicitly outside the analyst's domain
GEV and CEG carry zero analyst mentions, so they cannot rise above radar however load-bearing they are
